question.:question/problem:
Find the general nonzero real solution to the differential equation

$$
\frac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x}- y=\sqrt{y}.
$$ Take $y>0$. For even powers and powers of $2/3$ in the choices, retain only intervals where the base is positive. Choose constants and intervals on which the displayed expressions are real and finite.

{{selection}}
question.:question/worked-solution:
This is a Bernoulli equation with

$$\begin{aligned}p(x)&=-1\\ q(x)&=1\\ n&=\frac{1}{2}.\end{aligned}$$

Divide by $y^{\frac{1}{2}}$ and set $z=y^{\frac{1}{2}}$. The chain rule gives

$$\frac{\mathrm{d}z}{\mathrm{d}x}=\frac{1}{2 \cdot \sqrt{y}}\frac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x}.$$

Hence the linear equation in standard form is

$$\frac{\mathrm{d}z}{\mathrm{d}x}+\left(- \frac{1}{2}\right)z=\frac{1}{2}.$$

An integrating factor is

$$I(x)=e^{\int - \frac{1}{2}\,\mathrm{d}x}=e^{- \frac{\left(x+1\right)}{2}}.$$

Multiplying through and using the product rule gives

$$\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}x}\left(e^{- \frac{\left(x+1\right)}{2}}\,z\right)=\frac{e^{- \frac{\left(x+1\right)}{2}}}{2}.$$

Integrating with respect to $x$, we obtain

$$e^{- \frac{\left(x+1\right)}{2}}z=- e^{- \frac{\left(x+1\right)}{2}}+C.$$

Thus

$$z=C \cdot e^{\frac{\left(x+1\right)}{2}} - 1.$$

Finally, substitute $z=y^{\frac{1}{2}}$ and solve for $y$:

$$y=\left(C \cdot e^{\frac{\left(x+1\right)}{2}} - 1\right)^{2}.$$

Here $C$ is an arbitrary real constant; exclude singularities and restrict to the stated real intervals. The displayed expression for $z$ must be positive because $z=y^{\frac{1}{2}}>0$.

question.:question/problem:
Find the general nonzero real solution to the differential equation

$$
\frac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x}- \frac{y}{\left(x+1\right)}=\sqrt{\left(x+1\right)} \cdot y^{2}.
$$

Work on an interval where $\left(x+1\right)>0$. Choose constants and intervals on which the displayed expressions are real and finite.

question.:question/worked-solution:
This is a Bernoulli equation with

$$\begin{aligned}p(x)&=- \frac{1}{\left(x+1\right)}\\ q(x)&=\sqrt{\left(x+1\right)}\\ n&=2.\end{aligned}$$

Divide by $y^{2}$ and set $z=y^{-1}$. The chain rule gives

$$\frac{\mathrm{d}z}{\mathrm{d}x}=- \frac{1}{y^{2}}\frac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x}.$$

Hence the linear equation in standard form is

$$\frac{\mathrm{d}z}{\mathrm{d}x}+\left(\frac{1}{\left(x+1\right)}\right)z=- \sqrt{\left(x+1\right)}.$$

An integrating factor is

$$I(x)=e^{\int \frac{1}{\left(x+1\right)}\,\mathrm{d}x}=\left(x+1\right).$$

Multiplying through and using the product rule gives

$$\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}x}\left(\left(x+1\right)\,z\right)=- \left(x+1\right)^{\frac{3}{2}}.$$

Integrating with respect to $x$, we obtain

$$\left(x+1\right)z=- \frac{2 \cdot \left(x+1\right)^{\frac{5}{2}}}{5}+C.$$

Thus

$$z=\frac{C}{\left(x+1\right)} - \frac{2 \cdot \left(x+1\right)^{\frac{3}{2}}}{5}.$$

Finally, substitute $z=y^{-1}$ and solve for $y$:

$$y=\frac{5 \cdot \left(x+1\right)}{5 \cdot C - 2 \cdot \left(x+1\right)^{\frac{5}{2}}}.$$

Here $C$ is an arbitrary real constant; exclude singularities and restrict to the stated real intervals.

question.:question/problem:
Find the general nonzero real solution to the differential equation

$$
\frac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x}- 3 \cdot \left(x+6\right)^{2} \cdot y=- \frac{3 \cdot \left(x+6\right)^{2}}{y^{4}}.
$$

Work on an interval where $\left(x+6\right)>0$. Choose constants and intervals on which the displayed expressions are real and finite.

{{selection}}
question.:question/worked-solution:
This is a Bernoulli equation with

$$\begin{aligned}p(x)&=- 3 \cdot \left(x+6\right)^{2}\\ q(x)&=- 3 \cdot \left(x+6\right)^{2}\\ n&=-4.\end{aligned}$$

Divide by $y^{-4}$ and set $z=y^{5}$. The chain rule gives

$$\frac{\mathrm{d}z}{\mathrm{d}x}=5 \cdot y^{4}\frac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x}.$$

Hence the linear equation in standard form is

$$\frac{\mathrm{d}z}{\mathrm{d}x}+\left(- 15 \cdot \left(x+6\right)^{2}\right)z=- 15 \cdot \left(x+6\right)^{2}.$$

An integrating factor is

$$I(x)=e^{\int - 15 \cdot \left(x+6\right)^{2}\,\mathrm{d}x}=e^{- 5 \cdot \left(x+6\right)^{3}}.$$

Multiplying through and using the product rule gives

$$\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}x}\left(e^{- 5 \cdot \left(x+6\right)^{3}}\,z\right)=- 15 \cdot \left(x+6\right)^{2} \cdot e^{- 5 \cdot \left(x+6\right)^{3}}.$$

Integrating with respect to $x$, we obtain

$$e^{- 5 \cdot \left(x+6\right)^{3}}z=e^{- 5 \cdot \left(x+6\right)^{3}}+C.$$

Thus

$$z=C \cdot e^{5 \cdot \left(x+6\right)^{3}} + 1.$$

Finally, substitute $z=y^{5}$ and solve for $y$:

$$y=\sqrt[5]{C \cdot e^{5 \cdot \left(x+6\right)^{3}} + 1}.$$

Here $C$ is an arbitrary real constant; exclude singularities and restrict to the stated real intervals.

question.:question/problem:
Find the general nonzero real solution to the differential equation

$$
\frac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x}+y=- \left(x+1\right) \cdot y^{3}.
$$

Work on an interval where $\left(x+1\right)>0$. Choose constants and intervals on which the displayed expressions are real and finite.

{{selection}}
question.:question/worked-solution:
This is a Bernoulli equation with

$$\begin{aligned}p(x)&=1\\ q(x)&=- \left(x+1\right)\\ n&=3.\end{aligned}$$

Divide by $y^{3}$ and set $z=y^{-2}$. The chain rule gives

$$\frac{\mathrm{d}z}{\mathrm{d}x}=- \frac{2}{y^{3}}\frac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x}.$$

Hence the linear equation in standard form is

$$\frac{\mathrm{d}z}{\mathrm{d}x}+\left(-2\right)z=2 \cdot \left(x+1\right).$$

An integrating factor is

$$I(x)=e^{\int -2\,\mathrm{d}x}=e^{- 2 \cdot \left(x+1\right)}.$$

Multiplying through and using the product rule gives

$$\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}x}\left(e^{- 2 \cdot \left(x+1\right)}\,z\right)=2 \cdot \left(x+1\right) \cdot e^{- 2 \cdot \left(x+1\right)}.$$

Integrating with respect to $x$, we obtain

$$e^{- 2 \cdot \left(x+1\right)}z=- \left(\left(x+1\right) + \frac{1}{2}\right) \cdot e^{- 2 \cdot \left(x+1\right)}+C.$$

Thus

$$z=C \cdot e^{2 \cdot \left(x+1\right)} - \left(x+1\right) - \frac{1}{2}.$$

Finally, substitute $z=y^{-2}$ and solve for $y$:

$$y=\pm\sqrt{- \frac{2}{- 2 \cdot C \cdot e^{2 \cdot \left(x+1\right)} + 2 \cdot \left(x+1\right) + 1}}.$$

Here $C$ is an arbitrary real constant; exclude singularities and restrict to the stated real intervals. Both signs are retained wherever the radicand is positive.

question.:question/problem:
Find the general nonzero real solution to the differential equation

$$
\left(x+1\right)\,\frac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x}+y=- \left(x+1\right)^{2} \cdot y^{\frac{3}{4}}.
$$

Work on an interval where $\left(x+1\right)>0$. Take $y>0$. For even powers and powers of $2/3$ in the choices, retain only intervals where the base is positive. Choose constants and intervals on which the displayed expressions are real and finite.

{{selection}}
question.:question/worked-solution:
First, rearrange and divide by the coefficient of the derivative:

$$\frac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x}+\frac{y}{\left(x+1\right)}=- \left(x+1\right) \cdot y^{\frac{3}{4}}. $$

This is a Bernoulli equation with

$$\begin{aligned}p(x)&=\frac{1}{\left(x+1\right)}\\ q(x)&=- \left(x+1\right)\\ n&=\frac{3}{4}.\end{aligned}$$

Divide by $y^{\frac{3}{4}}$ and set $z=y^{\frac{1}{4}}$. The chain rule gives

$$\frac{\mathrm{d}z}{\mathrm{d}x}=\frac{1}{4 \cdot y^{\frac{3}{4}}}\frac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x}.$$

Hence the linear equation in standard form is

$$\frac{\mathrm{d}z}{\mathrm{d}x}+\left(\frac{1}{4 \cdot \left(x+1\right)}\right)z=- \frac{\left(x+1\right)}{4}.$$

An integrating factor is

$$I(x)=e^{\int \frac{1}{4 \cdot \left(x+1\right)}\,\mathrm{d}x}=\sqrt[4]{\left(x+1\right)}.$$

Multiplying through and using the product rule gives

$$\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}x}\left(\sqrt[4]{\left(x+1\right)}\,z\right)=- \frac{\left(x+1\right)^{\frac{5}{4}}}{4}.$$

Integrating with respect to $x$, we obtain

$$\sqrt[4]{\left(x+1\right)}z=- \frac{\left(x+1\right)^{\frac{9}{4}}}{9}+C.$$

Thus

$$z=\frac{C}{\sqrt[4]{\left(x+1\right)}} - \frac{\left(x+1\right)^{2}}{9}.$$

Finally, substitute $z=y^{\frac{1}{4}}$ and solve for $y$:

$$y=\left(\frac{C}{\sqrt[4]{\left(x+1\right)}} - \frac{\left(x+1\right)^{2}}{9}\right)^{4}.$$

Here $C$ is an arbitrary real constant; exclude singularities and restrict to the stated real intervals. The displayed expression for $z$ must be positive because $z=y^{\frac{1}{4}}>0$.

question.:question/problem:
Find the general nonzero real solution to the differential equation

$$
\left(x+1\right)^{2}\,\frac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x}=- \left(x+1\right) \cdot y - \frac{1}{\sqrt{y}}.
$$

Work on an interval where $\left(x+1\right)>0$. Take $y>0$. For even powers and powers of $2/3$ in the choices, retain only intervals where the base is positive. Choose constants and intervals on which the displayed expressions are real and finite.

{{selection}}
question.:question/worked-solution:
First, rearrange and divide by the coefficient of the derivative:

$$\frac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x}+\frac{y}{\left(x+1\right)}=- \frac{1}{\left(x+1\right)^{2} \cdot \sqrt{y}}. $$

This is a Bernoulli equation with

$$\begin{aligned}p(x)&=\frac{1}{\left(x+1\right)}\\ q(x)&=- \frac{1}{\left(x+1\right)^{2}}\\ n&=- \frac{1}{2}.\end{aligned}$$

Divide by $y^{- \frac{1}{2}}$ and set $z=y^{\frac{3}{2}}$. The chain rule gives

$$\frac{\mathrm{d}z}{\mathrm{d}x}=\frac{3 \cdot \sqrt{y}}{2}\frac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x}.$$

Hence the linear equation in standard form is

$$\frac{\mathrm{d}z}{\mathrm{d}x}+\left(\frac{3}{2 \cdot \left(x+1\right)}\right)z=- \frac{3}{2 \cdot \left(x+1\right)^{2}}.$$

An integrating factor is

$$I(x)=e^{\int \frac{3}{2 \cdot \left(x+1\right)}\,\mathrm{d}x}=\left(x+1\right)^{\frac{3}{2}}.$$

Multiplying through and using the product rule gives

$$\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}x}\left(\left(x+1\right)^{\frac{3}{2}}\,z\right)=- \frac{3}{2 \cdot \sqrt{\left(x+1\right)}}.$$

Integrating with respect to $x$, we obtain

$$\left(x+1\right)^{\frac{3}{2}}z=- 3 \cdot \sqrt{\left(x+1\right)}+C.$$

Thus

$$z=\frac{C}{\left(x+1\right)^{\frac{3}{2}}} - \frac{3}{\left(x+1\right)}.$$

Finally, substitute $z=y^{\frac{3}{2}}$ and solve for $y$:

$$y=\left(\frac{C}{\left(x+1\right)^{\frac{3}{2}}} - \frac{3}{\left(x+1\right)}\right)^{2/3}.$$

Here $C$ is an arbitrary real constant; exclude singularities and restrict to the stated real intervals. The displayed expression for $z$ must be positive because $z=y^{\frac{3}{2}}>0$.
